name: Matsés
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Matses has an alternating stress system where either all odd or all even syllables (counting left to right) in a (phonological) word are stressed (for phonetic characterization of stress see §2.7.1). The even- vs. odd-stressed pattern is lexically determined on all roots (this lexical stress can be shifted by some morphophonological processes; §2.6.5). Words composed of identical segment sequences can contrast with respect to being odd-stressed ... vs. even stressed ... [p.97] ... even-stressed roots and words are roughly three or four times more common than odd-stressed words. [p.183:] The stress system is quantity insensitive (i.e., not sensitive to syllable weight) ... (284) a. [tʃú.wa] 'heat up' b. [tʃu.wá] 'miss'
new_statements.citation: Fleck, David W. 2003. A Grammar of Matses. PhD dissertation, Rice University, Houston.
new_statements.locator: §2.2.3 'Phonemic stress', p. 97 (PDF p. 119); with §2.7.1 'Word-level stress', pp. 182-185 (PDF pp. 204-207)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Held file (1279-pp UMI scan, no text layer, fetched sources from etnolinguistica.org; present). I rendered PDF p. 119 (printed p. 97) and PDF p. 205 (printed p. 183) and read them visually, plus the held scanned of pp. 97-98, 165-166, 181-187. At §2.2.3 'Phonemic stress', p. 97, the text reads exactly: 'Matses has an alternating stress system where either all odd or all even syllables (counting left to right) in a (phonological) word are stressed (for phonetic characterization of stress see §2.7.1). The even- vs. odd-stressed pattern is lexically determined on all roots (this lexical stress can be shifted by some morphophonological processes; §2.6.5). Words composed of identical segment seq…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Binary alternating (every-other-syllable), quantity-insensitive stress across the phonological word; each root is lexically specified as odd-stressed (1st, 3rd, 5th... = trochaic from the left) or even-stressed (2nd, 4th, 6th... = iambic from the left), with even-stressed the default/majority pattern (3-4x more common, also imposed on loans and lexicalized forms); once the status of the first syllable is known, all other stresses follow regardless of suffixes. Phonetic correlates: vowel length and pitch.
new_statements.secondary_stress: All alternate syllables are stressed; 'The rightmost word-level stress seems to be the strongest, but not very noticeably so... so I do not distinguish between primary and secondary word-level stress' (p. 185).
new_statements.exceptions: Prefixation shifts the stress of even-stressed roots but not odd-stressed ones (stress contrast can be neutralized, §2.6.5 pp. 165-168); monosyllabic roots are intrinsically stressed or unstressed, revealed under suffixation (tad 'plane' vs tsad 'sit', p. 185); verbs ending in /ke/ or /ka/ never stress that syllable and always stress the preceding one (p. 186); reduplicated forms and onomatopoeic animal names with reduplicated parts form two phonological words and do not follow the alternation (pp. 186-187, §2.8); Spanish loans often adapted to even-stressed pattern (§2.10). Footnote 37 p. 183: closely related Chiankuëshbo shows the opposite preference (odd-stressed more common).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (root + suffixes/enclitics; alternation does not carry across words in a phrase, p. 187). Separately, utterance-level stress falls on the last syllable of the utterance regardless of word stress and can mask word stress in citation forms; Fleck elicited words in non-final position (p. 182, 187).
new_statements.identity_note: Fleck 2003 describes Matses as spoken by the Peruvian Matses communities (Gálvez/Yaquerana rivers, e.g. Nuevo San Juan), i.e. mats1244 proper; his footnote 37 (p. 183) contrasts it with Chiankuëshbo (a closely related Mayoruna variety spoken by a captive woman), which prefers odd-stressed roots. Dorigo de Carvalho's work concerns Brazilian (Javari) Matsés of the same language.
